sources.news_title: Faulty router, aging infrastructure blamed in US flight stoppage
sources.text:
A single faulty router may have triggered the nationwide ground stop ordered by the Federal Aviation Administration on Friday, underscoring the dangers posed by the US’ outmoded technological infrastructure.
The issue reportedly occurred as a contractor was replacing copper wiring, a scenario that experts have long warned of: A 2023 review warned that “system risk could quickly reach unacceptable levels” due to inadequate repairs. The US transportation secretary called for $50 billion to prevent a recurrence.
“There are many parts of airline and aviation technology that are no longer fit due to their age,” an industry analyst told CNN, likening it to keeping a 30-year-old car running. One air traffic controller said colleagues had resorted to purchasing replacement parts on eBay.

sources.news_title: Yikes: FAA Union Claims Nationwide Ground Stop Was Totally Avoidable
sources.text:
On Friday, we saw a nationwide ground stop that lasted for around four hours, making it the longest ground stop that we’ve seen in the country in over 25 years, since 9/11. This is of course a major screw-up, and it’ll likely take some time before an investigation fully reveals what the root cause of this was.
So far, the response from Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has been downright pitiful, and that’s the polite way of putting it. Along those lines, the union representing workers at the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is suggesting that this might’ve been completely avoidable, because unlike in the past, no risk assessment was performed prior to the mistake that caused this mess.
Duffy can’t keep story straight, but is desperate to blame
On Friday night, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin held a press conference to update people on the state of the shutdown. The whole thing felt to me like an SNL skit, because Duffy and Mullin couldn’t even keep their narratives straight, and the whole message was so tone deaf.
Rather than thanking the public for their patience, Duffy went on a rant demanding $50 billion from Congress, suggesting it’s their fault that they haven’t given Trump money for the past year. On Friday night, Duffy suggested the following was the reason that our skies shut down:
“What happened is that our switches, actually got overloaded with data, and they went down… I shouldn’t say they went down… they started to give us inconsistency with the data from those routers, and because of that, we shut the system down.”
So he suggested that this was because of switches being overloaded due to how outdated the system is, which of course raised lots of questions about what made Friday different than any other day, in terms of the system being overloaded. Not surprisingly, he didn’t have a good answer, because he was just talking out of his you-know-what.
Less than 24 hours later, Duffy switched his tune, explaining the situation as follows:
In at least one of our remote FAA locations, a contractor was doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunications lines from old copper wire and they were bringing it over to fiber. That contractor that does the work for us is L3Harris. They are our legacy provider, they’ve been working for the FAA for over 20 years.”
“What we are working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error or installer error from L3Harris, or did they install a faulty router.”
So on Friday, the problem was that the switches got overloaded due to how old the system was, and Duffy used that to essentially make the press conference a $50 billion demand to modernize air traffic control (which I’m all in favor of, for the record, if done correctly, but this doesn’t seem to be the time or place for this). Then on Saturday, it was a mess up by a contractor.
Does anyone remember when press briefings during a period of crisis were about sharing facts, and not just making random stuff up, and sharing theories that suit narratives? Those were the days…
FAA union says there was no oversight for this project
This is way beyond my area of expertise, but I’m sure I’m not alone in wondering how one contractor can make a mistake that just shuts down our entire aviation ecosystem? Shouldn’t there be a little more oversight so that such a major mistake can’t happen?”
This is where it gets interesting. PASS (“Professional Aviation Safety Specialists”) is the union representing 11,000 workers at the FAA. According to the union, historically projects like this would’ve been overseen by FAA employees with a risk assessment and more coordination, but that hasn’t been happening anymore. Here’s the statement:
The issue was isolated to two contractor owned and maintained routers that were being updated mid-day. Historically contractors have followed a protocol where FAA employees conduct a risk assessment and coordinate the maintenance of the system or equipment. PASS-represented technicians were not involved in the upgrades that led to the ground stop yesterday.
PASS fully supports the administration’s efforts to modernize the nation’s air traffic control system. It must be recognized by the FAA that modernization will move more quickly with fewer disruptions if PASS is fully engaged.The employees represented by the union are on the front lines and they have the skills and expertise to make the Brand New Air Traffic Control System (BNATCS) a reality. These employees should receive training on new equipment and could ensure more robust installation and optimization—if the workforce were properly staffed.
So a big question is when did FAA technicians stop being involved in these kinds of projects, in terms of coordination and risk assessment?
We don’t know to what extent this is related, but it of course has to be pointed out that in early 2025, Elon Musk’s DOGE (“Department of Government Efficiency”) laid off approximately 400 FAA employees. There wasn’t much transparency about who was laid off, though reports suggested that it included those tasked with aircraft safety inspections, and repairing air traffic control facilities.
One would hope that it will be investigated whether there’s any link here between the lack of oversight of projects like this, and the job cuts at the FAA.
Bottom line
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has done an abhorrent job handling the nationwide air traffic control shutdown, in my opinion.
On Friday night, he took the time to come up with a random, convenient theory as to what happened, to suit his narrative. He demanded $50 billion from Congress (which Republicans have had control of for the past two years), and expressed no sympathy for the public that has been impacted by all of this. Then less than 24 hours later, he blamed contractors, saying they messed up some wire upgrades.
Understandably, we’re all wondering how the heck an upgrade to wiring in one place could shut down our entire air traffic system. The union representing FAA employees is suggesting that historically these projects would be overseen by FAA employees, and would also include a risk assessment, but they insist no FAA employees were involved here.
Duffy is right about one thing — there was definitely some incompetence here…

sources.news_title: Who is L3Harris? Secretary Duffy points to contractor as possible cause of FAA outage
sources.text:
Who is L3Harris? Secretary Duffy points to contractor as possible cause of FAA outage
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday that a technical problem may have developed while FAA contractor L3Harris was upgrading a telecommunications line, triggering Friday’s nationwide ground stop.
What they're saying:
"At least one of our remote FAA locations, a contractor was doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from old copper wire, and they were bringing it over to fiber. That contractor that does the work for us is L3Harris. They're a legacy provider. They've been working for the FAA for over 20 years. … The network that we use at the FAA to control the airspace — L3Harris actually owns that network," Duffy said Saturday.
Dig deeper:
Duffy said a router at the location became overwhelmed by a surge of data as the contractor replaced copper lines with fiber-optic cables. The disruption then spread to routers at other FAA air traffic control facilities across the country.
RELATED: US flights to return to normal Sunday after ground stop canceled 1,000s of flights, FAA says
The other side:
L3Harris told Fox News Digital in a statement that it was assisting with the FAA’s investigation.
"L3Harris has been modernizing the communications infrastructure supporting the National Airspace System in close coordination with the FAA," the company wrote. "With safety and reliability as our highest priorities, L3Harris, together with its telco partners and the FAA, has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system."
The company said it was "supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel," adding that it "takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously."
Why you should care:
Duffy said the FAA and Transportation Department were investigating whether the disruption resulted from an installation mistake or a defective router.
"What we're working to determine was whether we had incompetence — meaning was it user error or installation error from L3Harris — or did they install a faulty router? We haven't determined what the fault was. Was it the router, or were they not doing great work for us at L3Harris," he said.
RELATED: Hochul calls for Transportation Secretary Duffy's resignation, firing after FAA ground stop
Asked whether the government’s lead systems investigator oversaw the work that preceded the network failure, Duffy pointed to the contractor.
"So this is L3Harris," he replied.
"It's our legacy telecom network. It's owned by L3Harris. With our new architecture, with the money that we're requesting, we will work with the greatest telecom companies in the world, which will be AT&T, Verizon and Lumen. They're all working with us on the new architecture," Duffy said. "But in the meantime, until I can build that, I'm stuck with L3Harris, who owns this network."
The backstory:
L3Harris has worked on FAA telecommunications since 2002 and supplies technology to a range of government customers.
According to its website, the company provides advanced targeting and ordnance systems to the Defense Department, along with weapons-related components and electronic systems for military use. Its products include ignition safety devices, proximity sensors and electronic fuzes.
L3Harris is also one of the U.S. military’s largest suppliers of tactical radios and other communications equipment.
The publicly traded company’s major institutional shareholders include BlackRock, with a 10.21% stake; State Street, with 5.1%; and Vanguard, with just under 12% held through Vanguard Capital Management LLC and Vanguard Portfolio Management LLC.
L3Harris reported $6.1 billion in revenue for the third quarter of 2026, according to its quarterly earnings report.
The company was established in 2019 through the merger of Harris Corporation and L3 Technologies.
The FAA and Transportation Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment from FOX Business.
The Source: FOX Business contributed to this report. Information in this story came from Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s Saturday news conference, an L3Harris statement provided to Fox News Digital, the company’s website and its third-quarter 2026 earnings report. FOX Business also sought comment from the FAA and Transportation Department, which did not immediately respond. This story was reported from Los Angeles.

sources.news_title: EXPOSED: Sec. Duffy Points Finger at Federal Contractor L3Harris in FAA Outage
sources.text:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Saturday identified L3Harris Technologies, a legacy federal contractor that has worked with the FAA for more than two decades, as a possible cause of the catastrophic router failure that forced a nationwide ground stop on Friday, Nov. 13 — halting flights across the country for more than four hours and stranding passengers just weeks before Thanksgiving.
Speaking at a news conference, Duffy said the trouble began at a remote FAA location where L3Harris was performing routine maintenance — switching telecommunications lines from aging copper wire to fiber optic cable. "That contractor that does the work for us is L3Harris. They're a legacy provider. They've been working for the FAA for over 20 years," Duffy said. "The network that we use at the FAA to control the airspace — L3Harris actually owns that network."
According to Duffy, as the conversion work proceeded, the FAA's router at that location began experiencing a flood of data, overwhelming the system. The issue quickly spread to routers at other FAA air traffic control systems nationwide, disrupting communications and radar feeds. The FAA issued the ground stop shortly after 3:36 p.m. ET. It was lifted at 8:15 p.m., but Duffy warned that delays and cancellations would continue for days as carriers repositioned aircraft and crews.
It is not yet known whether the failure stemmed from an installation error or a faulty router, Duffy said. Investigators are still working to determine the cause.
L3Harris, in a statement to Fox News Digital, said it is supporting the FAA's investigation. "L3Harris has been modernizing the communications infrastructure supporting the National Airspace System in close coordination with the FAA," the company wrote. "With safety and reliability as our highest priorities, L3Harris, together with its telco partners and the FAA, has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system." The company added that it is "supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel."
The ground stop drew immediate political fire. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul called on Duffy to resign over the incident, a demand that comes as the FAA chief, Bryan Bedford, has publicly apologized to travelers. Meanwhile, Duffy used the episode to press Congress for $50 billion to overhaul what he described as outdated routers and decades-old technology. "You will continue to see some delays and cancellations as carriers reschedule flights and reposition aircraft and crews where they are needed most," Duffy said on social media.
As Next News Network reported on X, Duffy said Friday's nationwide ground stop hit during the copper-to-fiber upgrade at a remote FAA site, when a router began flooding the network. Investigators are eyeing L3Harris and faulty gear. Another post noted that Hochul is demanding Duffy's resignation as the blame game escalates.
L3Harris Technologies, headquartered in Melbourne, Florida, is a major aerospace and defense contractor that has long handled communications infrastructure for the FAA. The company's work on the National Airspace System has been ongoing for years, and Duffy said the copper-to-fiber conversion has been occurring for decades. Whether the company bears responsibility for Friday's chaos — or whether the fault lies with the agency's aging equipment — will be a central question in the coming investigation.
Our Take
Here's what the Washington establishment won't tell you: this outage didn't happen because of one router or one contractor. It happened because the federal government has spent decades treating critical infrastructure like a piggy bank for everything except actual maintenance. L3Harris may have been holding the wrench when the system broke, but the FAA's copper-wire dinosaur has been creaking along for years while politicians patted themselves on the back for passing bloated budgets that never reached the routers.
Secretary Duffy is right to demand answers — and right to demand $50 billion for a real overhaul. But don't expect the same Democrats who want his head on a platter to lift a finger to fund the fix. Gov. Hochul's call for his resignation is pure political theater. Where was her outrage when the system was failing under the Biden administration's watch? The American people deserve a safe, modern air travel system, not a patchwork of legacy contractors and political scapegoats. The question is: will Congress act, or will they just wait for the next ground stop?

US aviation shutdown: 20,000 flights hit as FAA's ageing technology faces a fresh test after suspected router failure
sources.text:
WASHINGTON: A massive, nearly five-hour shutdown of the US aviation system that has disrupted more than 20,000 flights since Friday may have been the fault of a single router installed by government contractor L3Harris, government officials said Saturday.
The incident is the latest painful example of the aging US air traffic control telecom system and the struggles to replace systems while keeping the old communications working.
The FAA's aging telecom systems in recent years have failed after errant fiber cuts, accidental deletion of files and a strong chemical smell caused by a melted component. The system will fail again until it is properly upgraded, officials said.
"This was an FAA system that didn't meet the moment," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday.
Duffy said on Friday L3Harris was conducting routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from old copper wire to fiber at at least one remote location. Officials told Reuters there may have been problems with routers installed in both Arkansas and Texas.
"We're working to determine whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error or installer error from L3Harris, or did they install a faulty router? We haven't determined what the fault was," Duffy said.
L3Harris said it took the issue seriously and was "supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel."
L3 noted it has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber-optic system.
The FAA spends $1 billion annually to maintain its old copper wire system and is racing to replace it with more modern fiber-based communications.
"We need L3Harris or whoever provided that router to us to do a better job," Duffy said, noting that "virtually every single institution in America has gone from copper to fiber, from analog to digital."
The issue began overloading communications at 17 of the FAA's 22 en route centers across the country, which prompted the FAA to issue a nationwide ground stop because it could not identify a root cause.
Duffy said the new routers started flooding other routers with over 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, which sparked communications issues with planes and radar at FAA facilities.
Bedford said the FAA had to take the action when it lost "the ability for those routers to communicate data." The FAA is still trying to understand the root cause of what went wrong.
The FAA said communications did not go down but led to instability in data at the centers. It did not lead to centers going dark. The routers being replaced are about 25 years old, Duffy said, and were supposed to be replaced in 2006.
NOT THE FIRST TIME
Small mishaps leading to catastrophic consequences are not new to the US air traffic control network. A 2023 FAA nationwide ground stop that lasted 90 minutes and disrupted 11,000 flights was caused by a government contractor unintentionally deleting files.
That led to the first nationwide ground stop since the hijacked airplane attacks on September 11, 2001.
Friday's outage hit as a surge in travelers began weekend travel. Noting the poor timing, Duffy said they would reevaluate when work is done at smaller facilities to prevent future disruptions.

A router installed during an FAA technology upgrade may have triggered a nationwide US aviation shutdown, disrupting more than 20,000 flights. Here is what went wrong and why America's ageing air traffic control system is under scrutiny.
A routine technology upgrade may have triggered one of the biggest disruptions to US air travel in decades, after a router installed by government contractor L3Harris potentially caused a communications failure that forced the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to halt nearly all departing flights across the country.
The nationwide ground stop on Friday, November 13, lasted almost five hours and disrupted more than 20,000 flights through cancellations and delays.
Although the FAA lifted the restriction later that evening, the impact continued into the weekend, leaving tens of thousands of passengers stranded and airlines struggling to restore their schedules.
By Saturday evening, airlines had cancelled more than 6,150 flights and delayed over 7,300, according to FlightAware. This followed approximately 9,200 cancellations and 7,500 delays on Friday.
The FAA expected operations to return largely to normal only by late Sunday.
What makes the incident particularly significant is that investigators are looking at a seemingly small piece of networking equipment installed as part of an effort to modernise America's ageing air traffic control infrastructure.
How did one router trigger a nationwide aviation shutdown?
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the problem was linked to routine maintenance being carried out by L3Harris, which is working on replacing old copper telecommunications lines with fibre-optic infrastructure.
During the upgrade, at least one new router installed at a remote facility may have triggered a chain reaction across the FAA's communications network. Officials told Reuters that problems may have involved routers installed in Arkansas and Texas.
According to Duffy, the new routers began flooding other routers with more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. This overloaded the network and caused instability in the data being transmitted across air traffic control facilities.
The disruption affected 17 of the FAA's 22 en-route centres, which manage aircraft travelling between airports and across different regions.
The FAA said its communications systems did not completely go down and its facilities did not go dark. However, the instability meant controllers could no longer reliably exchange data through the affected routers.
The agency could not quickly establish the root cause of the problem, prompting it to take the precautionary step of grounding departing flights nationwide.
Duffy said investigators were examining whether the failure resulted from user error, an installation mistake by L3Harris or a faulty router.L3Harris said it was taking the matter seriously and supporting the FAA's investigation. The company also said it had completed more than 70% of the planned conversion of the airspace communications network from legacy copper lines to fibre optics.

Airlines had to reposition aircraft, bring crews back into place and manage congestion at airports where planes had been waiting for departure slots or gates.

Tens of thousands of passengers were left waiting at airports across the country.

sources.news_title: Why a problem on the ground can affect flights thousands of miles away among other issues - The Boston Globe
sources.text:
Regional US air traffic control centers communicate using a complex network that’s “one of the largest telecommunications systems in the country,” and disruptions like those seen on Friday with an hourslong, nationwide grounding of flights can reverberate widely, according to an aviation expert.
Michael McCormick, a former airspace manager with the Federal Aviation Administration, said it could take days for airlines — many of which had to divert flights — to resume normal operations after officials lifted the grounding order. The order was lifted late Friday.
Here’s a look at what happened, how regional air traffic control centers work, how controllers communicate with pilots and why a problem on the ground can affect flights thousands of miles away among other issues:
Top official cites ‘intermittent’ gaps in communication system
The nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the ground stop that lasted more than four hours on Friday, Trump administration officials said Saturday in a press briefing.
A contractor had been working on replacing a section of the system’s old and discontinued copper wire with new fiber wire in a remote location on Friday afternoon, Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said Saturday. That kind of work has been happening across the country and across industries for decades, he said.
“Specifically, we had over 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds,” Duffy said. “And what that did was gave us issues with our communication with airplanes, and it also caused some disruption with our radar feeds. And when we see that, your safety is paramount, we shut down the airspace.”
Planes flying at the time of the ground stop were able to land safely using “well-known procedures” in place for such circumstances, Duffy said Friday.
The government has been working to overhaul the outdated technology air traffic controllers rely on since Congress approved $12.5 billion for the effort last year. Miles of old copper wires have been replaced with fiber optic lines, while old radio systems are gradually being replaced at airports. But the work is far from complete, and Duffy used the news conference on Friday and Saturday to urge Congress to provide more funding.
Regional air control centers play a key role in high-altitude flights
The FAA grounded flights nationwide Friday due to issues at regional air traffic control centers, an FAA notice said.
The US operates 22 regional air traffic control centers, managed by the FAA, and they oversee long-distance aircraft operating between departure and arrival airports, according to McCormick, associate professor and program coordinator in the Department of Applied Aviation Sciences at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. McCormick estimates these control centers take over flights at altitudes over 10,000 feet.
These centers, which operate in such places as Anchorage, Alaska, Houston and Indianapolis, are one of the three layers that guide pilots. The airport towers direct pilots during takeoffs at the 500-plus airports that have towers. Then, the so-called Terminal Radar Approach Control centers take over and guide pilots as they get further away from the airport. And then the regional control centers take over. When descending, the reverse happens, experts say.
Experts say that the controllers at the regional centers are sitting at radar displays and are responsible for only that airspace.
“As you fly, your flight is handed off from one controller to another controller,” said Stephen Creamer, president and CEO of the Air Traffic Control Association, a trade group for equipment manufacturers involved with air traffic control. “That handoff process is like taking the screen and the aircraft on one screen and making sure it’s on someone else’s screen before you send the communications over to that next controller and have the pilot start talking to them.”
Pilots use radio frequency to communicate
McCormick said the country’s regional, high-altitude air traffic control centers need to be connected to remote radio transmitter or receiver sites. That’s to allow for radio frequency coverage to communicate with the aircraft.
Those transmitter sites are connected to the centers via telecommunications systems, the likes of which are in the process of moving from copper wires to fiber optic lines. The two-way communication is important to ensure — among other things — that planes maintain safe spacing, he said.
“What is especially problematic in this case is that it’s what’s known as a rolling outage,” McCormick said. “In other words, it’s unpredictable and it may impact one air traffic control center now and then it gets better and then impacts another air traffic control center.”
But he and other aviation experts said that the FAA is now transitioning to what’s known as controller pilot data link — a digital, text-based messaging system that allows controllers and pilots to exchange routine clearances, instructions and requests through the data link instead of voice radio.
A problem on the ground can affect flights thousands of miles away
In September, Newark Liberty International Airport temporarily lost radar communications with aircraft, after a backup fiber optic line was inadvertently cut by railroad construction workers. That forced the FAA to immediately cancel hundreds of flights going in and out of the airport.
But airline experts say that scenario was different from what occurred on Friday. Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford told reporters Saturday that intermittent frequency instability affected as many as 17 of the 22 U.S. regional air control centers.
“The thing that was unique about this is that it was a type of failure that wasn’t local because it was part of the communication system,” said R. John Hansman, an aeronautics professor at MIT whose research includes information technology in aviation. “It propagated around the country.”
Andrew Charlton, an aviation consultant, said the “knock-on” effect is incredible.
“The aircraft doesn’t just fly from A to B and back to B and then stop,” he said. “It then moves on to C and then over to E and around and around and around. It is, of course, exacerbated if you’re talking about long-haul flights, international flights over the Atlantic or over the Pacific.”
Even with a complete outage, pilots can still communicate
Aviation experts say that pilots can still communicate with aircraft even during intermittent communications disruptions, noting as an example that many planes have satellite phone systems.
Hansman said pilots can still talk directly to other pilots in airplanes around them via radio. There is also equipment on board that tells pilots if airplanes are around them, he added.
If a control tower loses radio capabilities, it can also communicate with pilots with high intensity light beams, which send signals to pilots to alert whether it’s safe to descend, Hansman said.
“We have a number of backup systems that allow the airplanes to fly safely to the extent that air traffic control can still communicate directly with the radio,” he said.

Join our WhatsApp group
Subscribe to our Daily Roundup Email
Duffy told reporters the work was performed by longtime contractor L3Harris, which has managed the FAA’s telecommunications network for more than 20 years and owns much of the infrastructure connecting air traffic control facilities. The copper wiring being replaced was so outdated that production had been discontinued, forcing the switch from analog TDM systems to digital IP technology.
During the upgrade, a router being replaced began flooding the network with more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. The overload disrupted communications with aircraft and radar data feeds, prompting the FAA to issue the ground stop as a safety measure while more than 3,500 planes were in the air. All airborne flights landed safely.
“We have an incredibly old telecommunication system,” Duffy said, describing equipment that includes 1980s-era switches, routers and copper lines. Investigators are determining whether the failure stemmed from contractor error during installation or from a faulty router. Duffy said there is no evidence of a cyberattack.
The ground stop, the longest of its kind in 25 years, led to thousands of cancellations and delays. Flight-tracking data showed roughly 9,000 cancellations on Friday and more than 5,000 additional cancellations into Saturday, with recovery expected to extend through the weekend. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford has projected airlines will largely return to normal schedules by late Sunday.
Duffy has repeatedly urged Congress to provide tens of billions more in funding — most recently seeking $50 billion — for a full overhaul of the air traffic control system. He has warned that the aging infrastructure will continue to fail without a complete modernization. Officials noted that newer IP switches already installed under recent upgrades remained stable during the incident, while legacy equipment did not.
L3Harris said in a statement that it is supporting the FAA investigation and has completed more than 70% of planned copper-to-fiber conversions nationwide. The company described safety and reliability as its top priorities.

Wiring Upgrade Went Wrong, Duffy Says
|                                                       By                             Bob Cronin                                 withNewser.AI                                                                                   Posted Nov 14, 2026  5:00 PM CST                                                       | 
Air travel in the US may be crawling back to normal, but the nationwide ground stop ordered Friday is still punishing passengers. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday that the shutdown appears to be tied to either contractor error or faulty equipment, after a router overloaded during a switch from copper to fiber lines at a remote FAA facility. The malfunction flooded the system with connection attempts, disrupting communications and radar feeds, the Washington Post reports. "Our contractor didn't meet the moment or the equipment didn't meet the moment," Duffy said, per the AP. He said the FAA has worked with L3Harris for decades. Passengers around the country were sleeping in airports, scrambling for alternative transportation, or just waiting. The fallout includes:
- Cancellations: FAA chief Bryan Bedford said 4,000 to 5,000 of Saturday's roughly 41,000 flights were scrapped on top of the 12,000 on Friday, but he predicted schedules would stabilize by weekend's end. "The worst is behind us," Bedford said Saturday.
- Possible causes: Officials ruled out cyberattacks and AI tools as leading to the shutdown. Aviation safety experts blasted the nation's aging, understaffed air traffic system.
- Political response: Democrats, citing unspent upgrade funds, pledged aggressive oversight of the Trump administration's modernization push. Duffy called for more funding in his comments, per USA Today. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries called the shutdown "the latest in a series of unacceptable air travel incidents" under the Trump administration, per the New York Times.
- Train demand: A surge of traffic from people trying to book train trips apparently took down Amtrak's website on Friday, per the Times.
- Rental car crunch: Passengers who decided to rent a car and drive instead often hit a wall. Rental companies were turning people away, and customers complained that reservations weren't being honored. Even locations other than airports were sold out, per the Times. Unable to rent anything else for the trip from Las Vegas to Los Angeles, Jessica Whitney improvised, paying $281 for the use of a U-Haul truck—despite the fact that not only was she not moving, she didn't even have her luggage, which was stuck in Las Vegas. "The U-Haul agent thought it was hilarious," she said.
- Silent Trump: President Trump made no public comment as the national chaos unfolded, though he posted online about topics including tax incentives for film production. "This is what President Trump does," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday night. "He puts leaders in place, and he allows them to lead."
- Searching: Tonya Owens, 56, said Saturday morning that she'd been at the Indianapolis airport for hours with her family for a flight to Miami, where they're to board a cruise ship. When the chaos began, she said, her airline "gave our seats away." A career nurse, she managed to book with another airline but canceled when the one-way tab for her family turned out to be $1,600, per USA Today. "I've worked two jobs to make this happen," said Owens.

The answer was not a foreign attack, an artificial intelligence failure, or the separate Microsoft outage that had rattled businesses only a day earlier.
It was a breakdown inside the aging air traffic control network, and officials say one piece of equipment began hammering the system so badly that the safest option was to stop departures nationwide.
By Saturday morning, Duffy said planes were moving again and the airspace was safe, even as airlines worked through thousands of disrupted flights.

The overload produced intermittent problems in communications and radar feeds. With controllers unable to quickly isolate the source and thousands of aircraft already in the air, the FAA stopped departures across the country.
That is a stunning chain of events. A maintenance job involving old copper wiring and one overloaded router was enough to force the most sweeping American aviation safety action in decades.
The White House published the full official briefing in which Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford walked through the failure and the decision to ground departures. sources.text:
A massive, nearly five-hour shutdown of the US aviation system that disrupted more than 20,000 flights may have been the fault of a single router installed by government contractor L3Harris.
The incident is the latest painful example of the ageing US air traffic control telecom system and the struggles to replace systems while keeping the old communications working.
WATCH THE VIDEO ABOVE: US aviation chaos exposes outdated infrastructure
Know the news with the 7NEWS app: Download today
The Federal Aviation Authority’s ageing telecom systems in recent years have failed after errant fibre cuts, accidental deletion of files and a strong chemical smell caused by a melted component. The system will fail again until it is properly upgraded, government officials said.
“This was an FAA system that didn’t meet the moment,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Saturday.
Duffy said on Friday L3Harris was conducting routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from old copper wire to fibre at at least one remote location. Officials told Reuters there may have been problems with routers installed in both Arkansas and Texas.
“We’re working to determine whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error or installer error from L3Harris, or did they install a faulty router? We haven’t determined what the fault was,” Duffy said.
L3Harris said it took the issue seriously and was “supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the November 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel”.
L3 noted it has completed more than 70 per cent of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fibre-optic system.
The FAA spends $US1 billion ($A1.5 billion) annually to maintain its old copper wire system and is racing to replace it with more modern fibre-based communications.
“We need L3Harris or whoever provided that router to us to do a better job,” Duffy said, noting that “virtually every single institution in America has gone from copper to fibre, from analog to digital”.
Routers were meant to be replaced 20 years ago
The issue began overloading communications at 17 of the FAA’s 22 en route centres across the country, which prompted the FAA to issue a nationwide ground stop because it could not identify a root cause.
Duffy said the new routers started flooding other routers with over 1000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, which sparked communications issues with planes and radar at FAA facilities.
Bedford said the FAA had to take the action when it lost “the ability for those routers to communicate data”. The FAA is still trying to understand the root cause of what went wrong.
The FAA said communications did not go down but led to instability in data at the centres. It did not lead to centres going dark.
The routers being replaced are about 25 years old, Duffy said, and were supposed to be replaced in 2006.
Small mishaps leading to catastrophic consequences are not new to the US air traffic control network. A 2023 FAA nationwide ground stop that lasted 90 minutes and disrupted 11,000 flights was caused by a government contractor unintentionally deleting files.
That led to the first nationwide ground stop since the hijacked airplane attacks on September 11, 2001.
Friday’s outage hit as a surge in travellers began weekend travel.
The FAA received $US12.5 billion ($A18.5 billion) to upgrade its badly ageing air traffic control and telecom system from Congress and Duffy has asked for $US50 billion ($A74 billion) more for air traffic control and airports.

sources.news_title: FAA Ground Stop: Duffy Points to L3Harris Router Upgrade
sources.text:
A routine copper-to-fiber swap at a remote site may have flooded the Federal Aviation Administration’s network and halted every departure in the country for more than four hours. The administration’s explanation has shifted more than once, and the equipment that failed was due for replacement in 2006.
A router installed by government contractor L3Harris Technologies may have caused Friday’s nationwide ground stop, the longest halt to American air travel since the September 11, 2001, attacks, government officials said Saturday. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the cause is still open: “We’re working to determine whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error or installer error from L3Harris, or did they install a faulty router? We haven’t determined what the fault was,” he said, according to Reuters.
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) stopped all departures from U.S. airports at 3:54 p.m. Eastern Time on Friday, November 13, and lifted the order at 8:15 p.m., ABC News reported. By 11:30 that night, nearly 10,000 flights had been canceled, Reuters reported, citing the tracking site Flightradar24. The disruption carried into Saturday, when more than 5,000 flights within, into or out of the United States had been canceled by 2:48 p.m. Eastern, according to FlightAware figures cited by Yahoo News.
What the coverage has missed
Most coverage has framed Friday as a story about old equipment. That is half of it. By the administration’s own account, the failure began at the point where new equipment was being connected to old equipment, during a modernization program Congress has already funded, on a Friday afternoon heading into a weekend travel surge.
The official explanations have also moved. On Friday night, Duffy told reporters that “all of the new equipment that’s been deployed did not go down” and that “this is all the old legacy equipment,” the Associated Press reported. At the same briefing, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the FAA was installing “new equipment, new technology” and “it was overwhelming the older system.” In remarks reported by Reuters on Saturday, Duffy described new routers that flooded older routers with more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. The two versions can be reconciled, since the old routers were what failed and the new ones were what overloaded them. But the public was told three slightly different stories in under a day, and the root cause has not been established.
How the afternoon unfolded
Duffy said trouble began at 3:36 p.m. Eastern, when air traffic control centers experienced instability in radar and communications systems. Aviation Week reported that the FAA pointed to overloaded analog switches and routers. Eighteen minutes after the first instability, the FAA ordered every airport ground stopped “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”
The agency’s only written statement, posted on its newsroom page and labeled preliminary, said the stop followed “communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers.” Duffy’s post on X said the issue affected “all” of them. Reuters later reported that the problem overloaded communications at 17 of the FAA’s 22 en route centers, the large facilities that handle aircraft at cruising altitude between airports.
Duffy said that at no point did controllers completely lose radar or radio contact. “Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data and they started to give us inconsistencies in the data from those routers and because of that we shut the system down,” he said. More than 3,000 aircraft in the air at the time were landed safely, according to Mullin. At least 827 flights were diverted by 7:05 p.m. Eastern, according to the aviation analytics firm Cirium, as reported by the AP. Cirium also counted about 11,000 flights carrying more than 1.5 million passengers scheduled to leave U.S. airports after 4 p.m.
Is it really the longest since 9/11?
Yes, on the available record. Reuters and the AP both describe it as the longest nationwide ground stop since the 2001 attacks, which kept civilian airspace closed for days. The only other nationwide stop since then came on January 11, 2023, when the system that sends safety notices to pilots failed after a contractor unintentionally deleted files. That stop lasted about 90 minutes.
Reported durations for Friday vary between “four hours” and “nearly five hours.” Both are defensible. From the ground stop order at 3:54 p.m. to its lifting at 8:15 p.m. is 4 hours and 21 minutes. Counting from the first instability at 3:36 p.m., it is 4 hours and 39 minutes.
The contractor and the router
The L3Harris connection first appeared on Friday through unnamed sources. Reuters reported that the outage “appeared to be affecting a telecommunications network overseen by L3Harris Technologies, according to two airline officials.” Those officials were not named, and RSN found no independent confirmation of their account before Duffy addressed it publicly.
Duffy has since confirmed the L3Harris role on the record. According to Reuters, he said the company was doing routine maintenance to move telecommunication lines from old copper wire to fiber at one or more remote locations. He also said the routers being replaced are about 25 years old and were supposed to be replaced in 2006. “We need L3Harris or whoever provided that router to us to do a better job,” he said.
One further detail rests only on unnamed sources: officials told Reuters there may have been problems with routers installed in both Arkansas and Texas. Neither the FAA nor the Department of Transportation has confirmed those locations publicly, and RSN has found no independent confirmation.
L3Harris has not admitted fault. In a statement, the company said it was “supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel.” It said it has completed more than 70% of the planned conversion from copper to fiber. The administration put the figure at 68% on Friday, according to Reuters.
Cyberattack and AI questions
Mullin said there was “zero evidence” so far of a cyberattack or a rogue artificial intelligence system, though investigators had not ruled out either. “It appears this was mechanically driven. However, we’re still looking,” he said, adding that the National Security Agency was assisting the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). “This isn’t another 9/11. I cannot repeat that enough,” he told reporters, according to KSAT.
The AI question arose because of timing. On November 10, three days before the outage, the FAA announced it would use its Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) system in the airspace of all 22 centers. The FAA describes SMART as a cloud-based platform that pulls together 200 data streams to recommend schedules. Duffy said Friday’s failure was not linked to SMART. KSAT reported that SMART runs from one location near Washington and only sends recommendations to the centers. No evidence published so far ties SMART to the outage, and RSN does not suggest one.
Background: a system flagged for years
The weaknesses were documented well before Friday. In 2024, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) found that the FAA had classified 51 of its 138 air traffic control systems as unsustainable and another 54 as potentially unsustainable, Reuters noted. That is 105 of 138 systems, or about 76%.
In September 2026, a circuit failure at a Philadelphia facility, followed by a construction crew cutting the backup fiber line in New Jersey, delayed or canceled about 9,500 flights in a single day. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said at the time: “When it fails, we just don’t have the redundancy that we would get if we had a modern architecture.” The FAA spends $1 billion a year maintaining its old copper network, according to Reuters.
Modernization is not a new idea either. RSN covered President Trump’s air traffic control reform initiative in June 2017. Congress finally approved $12.5 billion for the overhaul in July 2025. Earlier on Friday, before the outage, the White House and the Department of Transportation asked Congress for another $30.1 billion, including $10.1 billion for air traffic control. By Friday night, Duffy was asking for $50 billion. “What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system,” he said. “Give us the money to fix it.”
Deep dive: money is not the only gap
RSN analysis: Duffy’s case for more money has a real foundation. A 25-year-old router that was due for replacement in 2006 is the product of roughly two decades of deferred spending under administrations and Congresses of both parties. But the record shows that funding is not the only weakness.
In September, the GAO warned that the FAA lacked a reliable cost estimate and an integrated master schedule for the modernization program. As of May, the agency was running 11,389 separate project schedules that were not coordinated with one another, raising the risk of repeated work, delays and cost overruns. The FAA aims to finish the first phase by December 2028.
Friday’s failure fits that warning. Work at one or more remote sites was able to destabilize communications at 17 en route centers, which suggests the network had no effective way to isolate a misbehaving device before it spread. Duffy himself acknowledged the timing was poor, saying the FAA would reevaluate doing network work at smaller facilities during the day. That is a management decision, not a budget line. Taxpayers are entitled to know who approved the timing of the cutover work, what testing preceded it, and what the L3Harris contract says about liability.
Stranded travelers are absorbing the cost in the meantime. Because the failure was the FAA’s and not the airlines’, carriers are not required to compensate passengers, Reuters reported, though travelers who cancel because of a long delay are entitled to refunds, KSAT reported. Bedford said Saturday that airlines were waiving their terms and conditions for affected travelers.
The other side
Democrats rejected Duffy’s attempt to put the blame on Congress. Sen. Tammy Duckworth of Illinois, the top Democrat on the Senate aviation subcommittee, wrote on X: “You’ve literally controlled Congress for the past two years.” Republicans do hold majorities in both chambers of the current Congress, and Senate Republicans re-elected John Thune as their leader this week. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries called the outage an “unprecedented breakdown” and said “American travelers deserve timely answers from the Trump Administration about how and why this happened.”
There is a fair defense of the administration too. The ground stop worked as designed. Faced with unreliable data and no identified root cause, the FAA kept aircraft on the ground rather than launch them into airspace where controllers might lose contact, and no one was hurt. Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo, a former United Airlines pilot, told the AP that without reliable communications “you’ve got to stop airplanes on the ground.” Lawmakers from both parties have said Congress will investigate.
What is established, disputed and not established
Established (on-record statements and data):
- The FAA stopped all U.S. departures from 3:54 p.m. to 8:15 p.m. Eastern on November 13, 2026, the longest nationwide ground stop since 2001.
- Nearly 10,000 flights were canceled by late Friday (Flightradar24) and more than 5,000 more by Saturday afternoon (FlightAware).
- Duffy said overloaded routers and switches caused unreliable radar and communications data, and that an L3Harris copper-to-fiber cutover was under way at a remote site.
- Mullin said there was no evidence of a cyberattack so far; the NSA is assisting DHS.
Disputed:
- Whether “all” en route centers were affected (Duffy on Friday) or 17 of 22 (Reuters on Saturday).
- Whether the failure stemmed from old equipment, new equipment, or the connection between them; officials have described it all three ways.
- Whether Congress or the administration bears responsibility for the pace of modernization.
Not established:
- The root cause. Duffy said officials have not determined whether it was installer error or a faulty router.
- The Arkansas and Texas router locations, which rest on unnamed officials quoted by Reuters.
- Any link to a cyberattack or to the SMART AI system. Officials say there is no evidence of either, but neither has been formally ruled out.
Sources: FAA General Statements (Nov. 10 and Nov. 13, 2026); Reuters, Nov. 13; Reuters analysis, Nov. 14; Reuters, Nov. 14 (L3Harris); Associated Press; ABC News; Aviation Week; KSAT; Yahoo News live coverage.

sources.news_title: US air travel should normalize by Sunday
sources.text:
Airlines canceled thousands of flights across the U.S. on Saturday as they worked to recover from a nationwide ground stop a day earlier that left passengers scrambling for seats and disrupted travel around the world.
The U.S. air travel schedule should be back to normal by the end of Sunday, two days after what was the nation's longest ground stop in 25 years, Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford told reporters in Washington on Saturday. He said airlines “will still have delays and cancellations” Saturday but promised that the “worst is behind us.”
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the problem began when contractor L3Harris Technologies Inc. was replacing a section of the air traffic control system’s old copper wire with new fiber wire, somehow causing the system to overload. The work led to “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, prompting the government to shut down air traffic for more than four hours.
Duffy said officials were investigating whether contractor “incompetence” or a faulty router was the cause. “Our contractor didn't meet the moment or the equipment didn’t meet the moment,” he added.
L3Harris said it was supporting the FAA in its investigation to “understand the conditions” that led to the ground stop.
“L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously,” it said in a statement.
The nationwide stop was the first since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system that sends notices to pilots malfunctioned, and the second since the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.
Andrew Charlton, an aviation consultant, said Friday's stoppage affected about a quarter of the 45,000 flights in the U.S. each day.
“The knock-on effect of that is incredible,” said Charlton, managing director of Aviation Advocacy. “The aircraft doesn’t just fly from A to B and back … and then stop. It then moves onto C and then over to E and around and around and around. It is, of course, exacerbated if you’re talking about long-haul flights, international flights over the Atlantic or over the Pacific.”
Thousands of flights delayed and canceled
At airports across the U.S. on Saturday, passengers were still scrambling to figure out how to get to their destinations. Some waited out the chaos in hotels, others sprinted to snag rental cars and bus or train tickets. Many were forced to camp out in airports.
Others got creative. Video in Seattle's airport showed a passenger serenading stressed out travelers with classical music. Stranded strangers participated in a cornhole tournament at the Lexington, Kentucky, airport. The singer T-Pain and the band Hoobastank were captured on video singing to passengers as they waited on commercial airplanes.
Dan Russell, 66, learned his connecting flight from Kona, Hawaii, to Fresno, California, was canceled a half-hour before boarding was scheduled in San Diego on Friday night. Hotels were full, so he and his wife waited at the airport for a rebooked flight.
“There’s nothing you can do,” Russell said, as his wife, Mary, tried to nap on his shoulder.
A cheerful Southwest Airlines gate agent at Dallas Love Field greeted passengers at dawn with, “Good morning, good morning,” then repeatedly said all flights were full and asked passengers to have boarding passes ready to help keep flights moving.
In Las Vegas, Korean Mexican influencer Sujin Kim, known online as Chingu Amiga, said her flight to Mexico was rescheduled for Saturday morning. “Many people ended up sleeping at the airport, too, but thank God we managed to find a room,” she said.
At the Newark, N.J., airport, Umi Egchi was trying to figure out when his flights would line up so he could return home to Japan.
“I’m not sure exactly what happened. I just want to go home,” said Egchi, who had a sleep mask on top of his head.
Sports teams that traveled for games this weekend adjusted game start times, and No. 19 Mississippi’s game at Oklahoma was delayed a full day to Sunday.
FlightAware, a website that tracks flights, said more than 5,100 flights within, into or out of the U.S. had been canceled Saturday.
Officials say no one was in danger during ground stop
Duffy reiterated Saturday that no one was in danger as more than 3,000 flights in the air at the time of the grounding order landed safely.
Trump administration officials also blamed Congress for failing to approve more funding to replace the decades-old technology that helps manage the U.S. air traffic. Duffy said that 70% of the system had been replaced with fiber optic wire but that his agency also needs new air traffic control towers and runways.
The FAA has replaced thousands of old copper wires with fiber optic lines and upgraded hundreds of radio systems as part of an overhaul that began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion in funding. Duffy and the White House are pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work.
“We have aging infrastructure throughout the airspace,” Duffy said, while stressing that flying remains safe. “You won’t get to your destination if we don’t think you can get there safely.”
In a moment that perhaps only further underscored the Transportation Department’s struggling systems, Duffy’s news conference Saturday morning began with audio troubles that forced last-minute microphone swaps.
Although Duffy said he had repeatedly spoken with President Donald Trump since the ground stop began, the president has largely been quiet on the topic. He has not spoken publicly on the matter, nor issued statements via social media, although he commented on other things. He spoke on the phone with a Fox News reporter, but that was not on camera.
Charlton, the aviation consultant, pointed to the difficulties of updating a system that can never shut down.
“What you’re watching here is trying to change the tires of your car when the car’s going at 80 miles an hour down the expressway, because nothing stops in aviation,” Charlton said.
Past problems have been linked to equipment failures
The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast. That disruption was linked to a construction crew cutting a fiber optic line.
Aging equipment was also blamed for brief radar outages last year that disrupted Newark airport.
Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said the difference Friday was the nationwide scale of the disruption, which left controllers unable to reliably talk to pilots.
“If you don’t have that ability, whether it’s because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you’ve got to stop airplanes on the ground and not put them in the air, where you’re going to risk not being able to communicate with them,” said Arroyo, a former United Airlines pilot.
___
Kruesi reported from Providence, Rhode Island. Associated Press journalists Jill Colvin in New York, Seung Min Kim in Washington, Josh Funk in Omaha, Nebraska, Elliot Spagat in San Diego, Bernice Bautista in Las Vegas, Marc Levy in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania and Hannah Fingerhut in Des Moines, Iowa, also contributed.

US air travel chaos as thousands of flights canned
The head of the US Federal Aviation Authority predicts air travel won't immediately return to normal as the aviation system gradually recovers from a nationwide flight shutdown that officials blame on routine maintenance gone awry.
As of 6:45pm on Saturday (10:45 AEDT Sunday), airlines had cancelled more than 6,150 US flights and delayed more than 7,300, according to FlightAware, an aviation website.
That followed about 9,200 flights cancelled and 7,500 delayed on Friday after the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop because of disruptions to air traffic communications. FlightAware said more than 530 flights scheduled for Sunday were already cancelled.
Federal Aviation Administration head Bryan Bedford said on Saturday he expected airline operations to largely return to normal by late on Sunday and apologised for the disruption.
The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop on Friday that halted nearly all departing flights for almost five hours. It was the longest nationwide halt to air travel since the attacks of September 11, 2001 and one of the single worst US travel days ever.
The issue prompted the White House to convene an emergency meeting in the Situation Room on Friday and federal agencies to scramble to determine if it was a cyberattack. But the problem was traced to FAA contractor L3Harris' installation of at least one new router at a remote facility, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Saturday.
"We're working to determine whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error or installer error from L3Harris, or did they install a faulty router? We haven't determined what the fault was," Duffy told reporters at a news conference.
L3Harris said it took the issue seriously and is supporting the FAA in its investigation. Its shares last traded down about four per cent after hours on Friday.
Duffy said the trouble began on Friday afternoon, when air traffic control centres experienced instability in radar and communications systems. The router issue led to data overloading other communications centres, officials said.
"We had over 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, and what that did was (it) gave us issues with our communication with airplanes, and it also caused some disruption with our radar," Duffy added.
The issue affected communications at 17 of the FAA's 22 en route centres, which control aircraft during the cruise portion of a flight. Bedford said the FAA ordered the ground stop in case a centre lost all communications. "No facilities went dark. Nothing was fully lost", Bedford added.
The FAA said it was doing additional testing with L3Harris to see if there are any additional risks.
Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and American Airlines all cancelled about 25 per cent of their flights on Saturday, while JetBlue cancelled nearly 45 per cent. Airlines have issued travel waivers allowing passengers to rebook flights for later dates without cost.
Though the FAA lifted the ground stop on Friday evening, the disruption for passengers was far from over, with tens of thousands of people stranded in airports. Airlines were trying to get flight crews and other personnel in position to resume flights.
Friday's disruption is the latest and most dramatic sign of strain on a US air traffic control system beset by aging technology, equipment and communications problems and a shortage of several thousand controllers.

That network problem spread fast enough to disrupt communications with aircraft and interfere with some radar feeds, according to Duffy.
The result was a nationwide ground stop that lasted more than four hours Friday and sent the airline system into chaos.
But one crucial question is still unanswered.
Officials have not yet determined whether the failure was caused by an installation mistake, user error, or a defective router.
Duffy said the work began as L3Harris was replacing an aging copper telecommunications line with fiber at a remote FAA facility.
The old line was being discontinued, making the conversion necessary. Duffy described the underlying job as a routine move from analog technology to a modern digital connection.
Something went badly wrong during that process.
The router involved in the change began sending more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, Duffy said. Other routers across the air traffic system were then overwhelmed.
Controllers began seeing instability in radar data and communications with aircraft.
At that point, the FAA chose the safest option and halted departures nationwide.

Duffy stopped short of declaring that L3Harris was definitively at fault.
He said the government is working to determine whether the contractor made a mistake or whether the router itself was faulty.
That distinction matters because L3Harris is not a minor vendor handling an isolated piece of equipment.
It operates the communications backbone connecting much of America’s air traffic control system.
L3Harris Technologies describes its FAA telecommunications operation as a mission-critical network delivering 29,000 voice, data, and video services to the agency. Its public materials say the managed infrastructure supports communications, navigation, surveillance, and air traffic management for facilities that must remain connected around the clock.
The company says it monitors more than 100,000 network devices and has historically maintained 99.9998 percent uptime.
An L3Harris program profile says the private network connects more than 4,400 FAA sites and is used to support air traffic management communications across the country.
Those connections carry far more than ordinary office traffic. They support the voice, surveillance, navigation, weather, and operational data that controllers and aviation facilities need to keep aircraft separated and moving safely.
L3Harris says its engineers, operators, and technicians manage and update those systems as an extension of the customer’s own staff.
In other words, when that network stumbles, the effects can travel far beyond a single airport.
L3Harris has been tied to the FAA telecommunications system for more than two decades.
L3Harris Technologies says Harris Corporation won the $3.5 billion FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure program in 2002. The company says the program ultimately connected more than 4,400 national and international FAA and Defense Department facilities, managed more than 26,000 services, and supported over 50,000 users.
That system was designed to reduce operating costs, strengthen network security, and connect thousands of FAA and Department of Defense facilities.
The company known today as L3Harris did not exist under that name until 2019, when Harris Corporation merged with L3 Technologies.
The combined company became one of the largest defense and communications contractors in the United States, with major businesses spanning space, missile systems, tactical communications, surveillance, electronic warfare, and aviation infrastructure.
The merger joined two companies already deeply embedded in federal contracting and put the FAA network inside a much larger national security business.
That history helps explain why Duffy called L3Harris a legacy provider and why replacing the network cannot happen overnight.
The stakes reach well beyond one routine maintenance job.

The company’s quarterly report said orders reached $19.3 billion, while full-year revenue was projected between $23.5 billion and $23.7 billion, underscoring how heavily federal agencies rely on its technology portfolio.
Growth came from its space, mission, communications, spectrum, and missile businesses, showing how much broader L3Harris is than the FAA contract now making headlines.
That scale gives the company enormous technical reach, but it also raises the level of accountability when a network it operates is tied to a nationwide aviation shutdown.
That makes the FAA investigation especially important.

The nationwide ground stop lifted at 8:15pm ET.
Here’s a breakdown of today’s timeline: 
– At 3:36 p.m. ET, @FAANews experienced telecommunications issues at facilities & TRACONs across the country 
– The FAA issued a ground stop out of an abundance of caution while 3,500+… https://t.co/PrmWktsHiP
— Secretary Sean Duffy (@SecDuffy) November 14, 2026

Duffy said the old analog switches and routers became overloaded with data, while newer IP-based equipment did not go down.
FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said officials had found no evidence that the incident was caused by a cyberattack, a foreign actor, or artificial intelligence.
The department said controllers did not lose every radar feed or every communications channel. The instability was serious enough, however, that officials could no longer accept the risk of launching more aircraft into the system.
That is why thousands of planes already in the sky were allowed to land under established safety procedures while new departures remained on the ground.
That does not make the failure less serious.
It means the investigation is focused on the infrastructure itself, the equipment installed during the conversion, and the work performed on the network.
L3Harris said Saturday that it is supporting the FAA’s investigation and takes the nationwide ground stop and its effects on travelers, airlines, and air traffic operations seriously.
The company also said it has completed more than 70 percent of the planned conversion from legacy copper lines to fiber in coordination with the FAA and telecommunications partners.
The irony is difficult to miss.
The work intended to make the network newer and more reliable may have exposed just how fragile the transition still is.
For years, federal leaders have warned that the air traffic control system relies on aging technology that is expensive to maintain and increasingly difficult to support.
President Trump and Duffy have pushed Congress to fund a complete rebuild rather than continue patching decades-old systems.
Today’s nationwide ground stop happened because our air traffic control system is operating on DECADES-OLD, analog equipment that simply cannot compete with the demands of the 21st century.⁰@FAANews is modernizing this aging infrastructure thanks to a $12.5 billion down… pic.twitter.com/nXUPHkdNdV
— Secretary Sean Duffy (@SecDuffy) November 14, 2026
U.S. Department of Transportation said earlier this month that the administration had replaced 69 percent of the copper wires in the air traffic system and installed 226 modern IP voice switches. The same update described a new display system being deployed at more than 400 FAA facilities so controllers can see operational updates, equipment disruptions, weather information, and safety alerts in one place.
Friday’s outage shows why every stage of that overhaul must be tested, isolated, and supervised with extraordinary care.
A single bad router or installation error should not be able to flood a nationwide network and force every commercial departure in America to stop.
The modernization effort also includes replacing floppy-disk systems, moving towers to electronic flight strips, upgrading radios, and giving controllers modern information displays.
Those improvements are meant to eliminate the brittle equipment and hard-to-replace parts that have accumulated over decades.
But modernization creates its own risk when old and new systems must operate together during a live transition. Friday’s failure is now a test of whether the FAA and its contractors built enough isolation and redundancy into that process.
Duffy has promised accountability once investigators determine exactly what happened.
That investigation now has to answer three questions clearly: what failed, who was responsible for the work, and why the system’s redundancies did not prevent one remote-site problem from spreading across the country.
Until those answers are public, L3Harris remains under intense scrutiny.
The company has spent decades helping run the network behind America’s skies.
Now the country is waiting to learn whether work on that same network brought those skies to a standstill.
