sources.news_title: Airport nightmares continue as FAA struggles to pinpoint blame for historic meltdown
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — The U.S. Department of Transportation was working Saturday to determine whether Friday’s air traffic control system meltdown resulted from human error or equipment failure as travelers across the nation continued to grapple with a cascade of flight delays and cancellations.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the crisis began when a contractor was performing routine maintenance at a remote FAA location to switch telecommunication lines from 1980s-era copper wire to a fiber line.
The new equipment began flooding other routers in the air traffic control system — sending more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds — causing radar and communications disruptions, he said. As a safety measure, the FAA decided to ground all planes for more than four hours.
It is unclear whether the contractor, L3Harris Technologies, or the piece of new equipment itself was at fault.
“This was an FAA system that didn’t meet the moment,” said Duffy. “A contractor didn’t meet the moment or the equipment didn’t meet the moment — and it caused the outages.”
A spokesperson for L3Harris said the company is supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the ground stop. L3Harris said safety and reliability are its highest priorities and that it takes the impact of Friday’s incident on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.
FAA Administrator Brian Bedford said he is hopeful airlines will be able to resume normal flight schedules by close of business Sunday.
There is no evidence that Friday’s system failure was caused by AI or any nefarious actors, Bedford said. He apologized to passengers impacted by the FAA’s decision to ground flights and emphasized that no lives were harmed during the crisis.
“I’m sorry that we put you through this, but we did it for the right reasons,” he said.
Duffy said the ground stop highlighted the need to continue modernizing the FAA’s “incredibly old” telecommunication system. Currently, around 70% of the system has been moved to a fiber network, but the remainder relies on copper wire, he said.
Duffy thanked President Donald Trump for securing a $12.5 billion investment in the FAA through his 2025 “Big Beautiful Bill” and called on Congress to approve an additional $30 billion funding request to continue modernizing the nation’s aviation infrastructure.
Chaos reigns at airports across America
On Saturday morning, thousands of planes were back in American airspace, but airlines warned it would take several days to recover and urged passengers to change their flights to later dates where possible. The FAA anticipates that 4,000 to 5,000 of the 41,000 flights scheduled in America on Saturday will be canceled, Bedford said.
On Friday, there were more than 7,400 flight delays within, into, or out of the United States and more than 9,000 cancellations, according to flight-tracking website FlightAware.
Leis Rodriguez’s flight from LAX to San Antonio at 6:30 p.m. Friday was among the thousands that were grounded. She and her sister were rebooked for a Saturday morning flight, but it was delayed, leaving them to sit for hours in the airport hoping they’d be able to board at some point.
“We have to rely on a lot of patience,” Rodriguez said. “Not knowing if your flight is going to be canceled is anxiety-producing.”
Despite the inconvenience and uncertainty, she’s glad the government took action and grounded flights on Friday.
“Safety is paramount, and I’d rather have this experience than have any kind of huge safety risk,” she said.
Sister Nyla Butler and Elder Zachary Woods, both missionaries with the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, were on the tarmac Friday in Melbourne when they got word of flights being grounded in the U.S. They eventually made it to LAX, but missed their connecting flights home to Alberta and Seattle, respectively.
On Saturday morning, the 20-year-olds wore their church name tags as they stood with their luggage in a line of hundreds of people hoping to rebook flights.
“There’s just been a lot of confusion, having no idea where we are, what line we’re supposed to be in,” Woods said.
Vivi Zhang, meanwhile, sat despondently with her luggage on a windowsill near a lengthy check-in line. Her 7 a.m. flight to Calgary was canceled, and the next available flight is Sunday. She said she was frustrated by the lack of support from airline staff.
“No food, no hotel voucher, anything,” she said. “They just said ‘not our fault.’”
Democrats outraged over handling of crisis
The ground stop sparked barbed political discourse over the initial lack of clear communication from White House officials and how a routine upgrade could generate such a disastrous impact on the FAA’s watch.
“The Transportation and Homeland Security leaders were slow to provide updates, and when they did speak, they didn’t have good explanations about what was happening, nor whether it would happen again,” Rep. George Whitesides, D-Calif., said in a Friday evening statement on X.
Whitesides, who was himself stuck in an airport for seven hours Friday, criticized the president for installing a Transportation Secretary with “basically no professional transportation experience in one of the most crucial jobs we have as a country.” Duffy is a former sports television personality, prosecutor, congressmember and CNN political contributor.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul called on Duffy to resign or Trump to remove him from his post.
“From chronic air traffic controller shortages to repeated communications breakdowns, serious lapses in our aviation system have become a pattern on Sean Duffy’s watch,” she said in a statement Saturday. “Through it all, he’s been more focused on starring in his own reality show than addressing the crisis at his agency.”
Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg questioned why an isolated equipment failure resulted in such a sustained disruption of the nation’s air traffic control system.
“The system has many redundancies in it so that normally, if there’s one point of failure, something else can catch it,” he said Friday, noting that when a system crashed under his tenure as secretary in 2023 the outage was shorter, lasting around 90 minutes.
“There were actually four different systems, and one of them went out, and another one could be brought online to cover,” he explained, “so it is not clear to me why that redundancy did not prevent an outage of this magnitude in terms of the scope and duration.”
Trump, who rarely shies away from the spotlight, did not comment on the unprecedented telecommunications outage Friday. When asked about the president’s silence at a Friday evening news conference, Duffy said that Trump was “fully engaged” behind the scenes.
On Saturday, Trump posted a quote from Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., on Truth Social that detailed the legislator’s political priorities, including getting Democrats’ support on a FAA funding bill.
Earlier in the day, Duffy called on Democrats and Republicans to unite and approve funding to finish modernizing the FAA’s air traffic control network and upgrade other aging infrastructure, such as towers and tarmac, at airports across America.

(Times staff writer Ana Ceballos contributed to this report.)

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said officials had found no evidence that the incident was caused by a cyberattack, a foreign actor, or artificial intelligence.
The department said controllers did not lose every radar feed or every communications channel. The instability was serious enough, however, that officials could no longer accept the risk of launching more aircraft into the system.
That is why thousands of planes already in the sky were allowed to land under established safety procedures while new departures remained on the ground.
That does not make the failure less serious.
It means the investigation is focused on the infrastructure itself, the equipment installed during the conversion, and the work performed on the network.
L3Harris said Saturday that it is supporting the FAA’s investigation and takes the nationwide ground stop and its effects on travelers, airlines, and air traffic operations seriously.
The company also said it has completed more than 70 percent of the planned conversion from legacy copper lines to fiber in coordination with the FAA and telecommunications partners.
The irony is difficult to miss.
The work intended to make the network newer and more reliable may have exposed just how fragile the transition still is.
For years, federal leaders have warned that the air traffic control system relies on aging technology that is expensive to maintain and increasingly difficult to support.
President Trump and Duffy have pushed Congress to fund a complete rebuild rather than continue patching decades-old systems.
Today’s nationwide ground stop happened because our air traffic control system is operating on DECADES-OLD, analog equipment that simply cannot compete with the demands of the 21st century.⁰@FAANews is modernizing this aging infrastructure thanks to a $12.5 billion down… pic.twitter.com/nXUPHkdNdV
— Secretary Sean Duffy (@SecDuffy) November 14, 2026
U.S. Department of Transportation said earlier this month that the administration had replaced 69 percent of the copper wires in the air traffic system and installed 226 modern IP voice switches. The same update described a new display system being deployed at more than 400 FAA facilities so controllers can see operational updates, equipment disruptions, weather information, and safety alerts in one place.
Friday’s outage shows why every stage of that overhaul must be tested, isolated, and supervised with extraordinary care.
A single bad router or installation error should not be able to flood a nationwide network and force every commercial departure in America to stop.
The modernization effort also includes replacing floppy-disk systems, moving towers to electronic flight strips, upgrading radios, and giving controllers modern information displays.
Those improvements are meant to eliminate the brittle equipment and hard-to-replace parts that have accumulated over decades.
But modernization creates its own risk when old and new systems must operate together during a live transition. Friday’s failure is now a test of whether the FAA and its contractors built enough isolation and redundancy into that process.
Duffy has promised accountability once investigators determine exactly what happened.
That investigation now has to answer three questions clearly: what failed, who was responsible for the work, and why the system’s redundancies did not prevent one remote-site problem from spreading across the country.
Until those answers are public, L3Harris remains under intense scrutiny.
The company has spent decades helping run the network behind America’s skies.
Now the country is waiting to learn whether work on that same network brought those skies to a standstill.

US: Duffy says 'incompetence' or bad tech to blame for flight haltings
November 14, 2026
US Federal Aviation Administration officials and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Saturday said that investigations are ongoing in an attempt to find the cause of the largest mass grounding of flights in the country in over 25 years.
Stranded passengers scrambled to find hotel rooms or buses and trains that could take them to their destinations, others hunkered down in the nation's airports in the first such nationwide grounding since January 2023 and the largest since the September 11, 2001, terror attacks.
International carriers were also forced to cancel flights to the US, and the massive backlog prompted, among other things, the rescheduling of dozens of college and professional sporting events — a staple of many Americans' weekends.
FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said that a total of 16,000 flights had been delayed on Friday and Saturday, adding that he hoped flight schedules would be back to normal sometime Sunday, saying the "worst is behind us."
Transportation Secretary Duffy seeks to deflect blame
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said no evidence of malfeasance had been found, before pointing his finger at numerous possible culprits, starting with the previous administration, then Congress and eventually settling on possible "contractor incompetence."
Duffy said the issue may have been a faulty router installed when workers from "legacy contractor" L3Harris replaced aged copper wire with new fiberoptic cable or that they had somehow caused a system overload while updating the wires.
During a press conference that was itself plagued with technical problems, Duffy said, "We're working to determine whether we had incompetence, meaning, was it user error or installer error from L3Harris, or did they install a faulty router? We haven't determined what the fault was," Duffy said, adding that either way, "Our contractor didn't meet the moment."
He was also asked why such complicated updates would be undertaken on a Friday afternoon when air travel is at its busiest rather than on a Saturday night, for instance, when far-fewer planes are in the air. He replied by saying the scheduling of such updates will be reevaluated moving forward.
Since the decision was made to update the very old infrastructure currently in use, Congress has approved $12.5 billion (€11.3 billion) to fund the changeover. The Trump administration had been seeking a further $30 billion to complete the job but Duffy on Friday called $50 billion instead, saying, "This is an emergency."
Who will compensate customers?
Despite the pain and frustration endured by customers, there is also a massive financial component to the groundings.
Since the groundings were ordered by the FAA, airlines are not legally responsible for compensating passengers whose flights were cancelled.
On Saturday, Administrator Bedford said the FAA is "working with aviation stakeholders" to make things right, saying, "everyone will either be reaccommodated (sic) on a flight or they'll get a full refund."
Investors are already beginning to calculate potential losses to airlines — which will compound the sting of sky-high fuel prices brought on by the Trump administration's war in Iran and the subsequent closure of the Strait of Hormuz — with shares of American, Delta and United Airlines falling between 1% and 2% late Friday.
Shares in JetBlue as well as contractor L3Harris were down 3%.

sources.news_title: Why problem on ground can affect flights thousands of miles away
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — Regional U.S. air traffic control centers communicate using a complex network that's “one of the largest telecommunications systems in the country,” and disruptions like those seen on Friday with an hourslong, nationwide grounding of flights can reverberate widely, according to an aviation expert.
Michael McCormick, a former airspace manager with the Federal Aviation Administration, said it could take days for airlines — many of which had to divert flights — to resume normal operations after officials lifted the grounding order. The order was lifted late Friday.
Here's a look at what happened, how regional air traffic control centers work, how controllers communicate with pilots and why a problem on the ground can affect flights thousands of miles away among other issues:
Top official cites ‘instability’ in communication system
New technology being added to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the ground stop that lasted more than four hours Friday, Trump administration officials said Saturday in a press briefing.
Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said a contractor had been working on replacing a section of the system’s old copper wire with new fiber wire, and that somehow resulted in the system overload. Duffy said officials were probing whether contractor “incompetence” or a faulty router was the cause.
“Specifically, we had over 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds,” Duffy said. “And what that did was gave us issues with our communication with airplanes, and it also caused some disruption with our radar feeds. And when we see that, your safety is paramount, we shut down the airspace.”
Planes flying at the time of the ground stop were able to land safely using “well-known procedures” in place for such circumstances, Duffy said Friday.
The government has been working to overhaul the outdated technology air traffic controllers rely on since Congress approved $12.5 billion for the effort last year. Miles of old copper wires have been replaced with fiber optic lines, while old radio systems are gradually being replaced at airports. But the work is far from complete, and Duffy used the news conference on Friday and Saturday to urge Congress to provide more funding.
Regional air control centers play a key role in high-altitude flights
The FAA grounded flights nationwide Friday due to issues at regional air traffic control centers, an FAA notice said.
The U.S. operates 22 regional air traffic control centers, managed by the FAA, oversees long-distance aircraft operating between departure and arrival airports. according to McCormick, associate professor and program coordinator in the Department of Applied Aviation Sciences at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. McCormick estimates these control centers take over flights at altitudes over 10,000 feet.
These centers, which operate in such places as Anchorage, Alaska, Houston and Indianapolis, are one of the three layers that guide pilots. The airport towers direct pilots at the takeoffs at the 500-plus airports that have towers. Then, the so-called Terminal Radar Approach Control centers take over and guide pilots as they get further away from the airport. And then the regional control centers take over. When descending, the reverse happens, experts say.
Experts say that the controllers at the regional centers are sitting at radar displays and are responsible for only that airspace.
“As you fly, your flight is handed off from one controller to another controller,” said Stephen Creamer, president of the Air Traffic Control Association, a trade group for equipment manufacturers involved with air traffic control. “That handoff process is like taking the screen and the aircraft on one screen and making sure it’s on someone else’s screen before you send the communications over to that next controller and have the pilot start talking to them.”
Pilots use radio frequency to communicate
McCormick said the country's regional, high-altitude air traffic control centers need to be connected to remote radio transmitter or receiver sites. That's to allow for radio frequency coverage to communicate with the aircraft.
Those transmitter sites are connected to the centers via telecommunications systems, the likes of which are in the process of moving from copper wires to fiber optic lines. The two-way communication is important to ensure — among other things — that planes maintain safe spacing, he said.
“What is especially problematic in this case is that it’s what’s known as a rolling outage,” McCormick said. “In other words, it's unpredictable and it may impact one air traffic control center now and then it gets better and then impacts another air traffic control center.”
But he and other aviation experts said that the FAA is now transitioning to what's known as controller pilot data link — a digital, text-based messaging system that allows controllers and pilots to exchange routine clearances, instructions and requests through the data link instead of voice radio.
A problem on the ground can affect flights thousands of miles away
In September, Newark Liberty International Airport temporarily lost radar communications with aircraft, after a backup fiber optic line was inadvertently cut by railroad construction workers. That forced the FAA to immediately cancel hundreds of flights going in and out of the airport.
But airline experts say that scenario was different from what occurred on Friday. Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford told reporters Saturday that intermittent frequency instability affected as many as 17 of the 22 U.S. regional air control centers.
“The thing that was unique about this is that it was a type of failure that wasn’t local because it was part of the communication system,” he said. “It propagated around the country.”
Andrew Charlton, an aviation consultant, said the “knock-on” effect is incredible.
“The aircraft doesn’t just fly from A to B and back to B and then stop,” he said. “It then moves onto C and then over to E and around and around and around. It is, of course, exacerbated if you’re talking about long-haul flights, international flights over the Atlantic or over the Pacific.”
Even with a complete outage, pilots can still communicate
Aviation experts say that pilots can still communicate with aircraft even during intermittent communications disruptions, noting as an example that many planes have satellite phone systems.
John Hansman, aeronautics professor at MIT whose research includes information technology in aviation, said that pilots can still talk directly to other pilots in airplanes around them via radio. And there's also equipment on the airplane that tells pilots if there are airplanes around them, he said.
If a control tower loses radio capabilities, it can also communicate with pilots with high intensity light beams, which send signals to pilots to alert whether it's safe to descend, he said.
“We have a number of backup systems that allow the airplanes to fly safely to the extent that air traffic control can still communicate directly with the radio,” said Hansman.

Who is L3Harris, the federal contractor Sec Duffy says may have caused the FAA outage?
Duffy questions L3Harris role in nationwide FAA ground stop as investigation unfolds
During a Saturday news conference explaining why the Federal Aviation Administration instituted a nationwide ground stop for all flights Friday, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy claimed a technical issue may have occurred while federal telecommunications contractor L3Harris was doing work on an FAA telecommunications line.
"At least one of our remote FAA locations, a contractor was doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from old copper wire, and they were bringing it over to fiber. That contractor that does the work for us is L3Harris. They're a legacy provider. They've been working for the FAA for over 20 years. … The network that we use at the FAA to control the airspace — L3Harris actually owns that network," Duffy said Saturday.
The secretary continued to explain that while L3Harris was working to move the system out of the analog copper wire infrastructure into a digital framework via updated fiber optic cables, the FAA's router at that location began experiencing a flood of data causing it to be overwhelmed — an issue that quickly spread to routers at other FAA air traffic control systems nationwide.
L3Harris, in a statement to Fox News Digital, said it was supporting the FAA's investigations.
"L3Harris has been modernizing the communications infrastructure supporting the National Airspace System in close coordination with the FAA," the company wrote. "With safety and reliability as our highest priorities, L3Harris, together with its telco partners and the FAA, has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system."
They added they are "supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel," noting L3Harris "takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously."
The Transportation Secretary said the FAA and Department of Transportation were working to determine whether L3Harris operator error caused the issue or if it happened because of a faulty router.
DUFFY SOUNDS ALARM OVER AGING FAA SYSTEM AFTER NATIONWIDE AIR TRAVEL SHUTDOWN
"What we're working to determine was whether we had incompetence — meaning was it user error or installation error from L3Harris — or did they install a faulty router? We haven't determined what the fault was. Was it the router, or were they not doing great work for us at L3Harris," he said.
Duffy also seemed to pin the blame on L3Harris when asked if the government's lead systems investigator oversaw the operation that led to the network failure.
"So this is L3Harris," he replied.
"It's our legacy telecom network. It's owned by L3Harris. With our new architecture, with the money that we're requesting, we will work with the greatest telecom companies in the world, which will be AT&T, Verizon and Lumen. They're all working with us on the new architecture," Duffy said. "But in the meantime, until I can build that, I'm stuck with L3Harris, who owns this network."
In addition to working with the FAA on telecommunications since 2002, the company has a wide range of technologies and government partners.
According to its website, L3Harris provides advanced targeting and ordnance systems to the U.S. Department of Defense, and develops advanced ancillary weapon and electronic systems for military applications.
Some of those applications include ignition safety devices, proximity sensors and electronic fuzes.
The company is also one of the largest suppliers of tactical radios and other communications equipment to the U.S. military.
L3Harris is a publicly traded corporation with majority shareholders including major asset managers such as: BlackRock, which owns 10.21%; State Street, which owns 5.1%; and Vanguard, which owns just under 12%, split between its Vanguard Capital Management LLC and Vanguard Portfolio Management LLC.
The company recorded $6.1 billion in revenue in the third quarter of 2026, according to its quarterly report.
L3Harris was formed in 2019 when defense and communications contractor Harris Corporation and L3 Technologies merged.

What Caused the US FAA Ground Stop and How Did a Copper-To-Fibre Switch Disrupt Flight Radar Feeds?
Investigators are examining possible contractor error or faulty equipment after a network disruption caused thousands of flight cancellations
A contractor's work replacing copper telecommunications lines with fibre may have triggered the US Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) ground stop on Friday, 13 November. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said investigators were examining whether contractor error or a faulty router disrupted communications and radar feeds. The exact fault has not been confirmed.
The ground stop was lifted after more than four hours, but the disruption carried on into Saturday, 14 November. FlightAware data showed 3,374 US flights cancelled by early Saturday morning.
Duffy said the problem began during routine maintenance at a remote FAA site. He named L3Harris Technologies, the FAA's long-time telecommunications contractor and the operator of its network, as the company carrying out the work.
How the Contractor's Network Upgrade May Have Triggered the Outage
According to Duffy, a router involved in the copper-to-fibre switch started flooding other routers across the air traffic control network. 'We had over 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds,' he said.
The network carries radar data and voice communications between FAA facilities, allowing controllers to monitor aircraft and communicate with pilots. As the connection attempts overwhelmed the network, controllers experienced inconsistent radar data and difficulties communicating with aircraft. A senior government official later told NBC News the system behind the outage had been identified and taken offline.
Investigators are examining whether the incident resulted from 'user error or installer error' or faulty equipment, Duffy said.
The FAA has been replacing old copper lines with fibre, 5G wireless and low-Earth-orbit satellite links. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told lawmakers in September that over 64 per cent of the copper-based network had been replaced by 1 September. Duffy put the figure at 69 per cent on Saturday.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said officials had found no sign of an attack but were not ruling one out. 'There's nothing completely certain right now. It doesn't appear that way,' he said.
Duffy said officials did not believe a foreign nation had attacked the network.
Flight Disruptions Spread Across the US and Canada
Controllers first noticed the inconsistent radar and communications data at 3.36pm Eastern time on Friday, according to Duffy. The FAA issued the ground stop at 3.54pm and lifted it at 8.15pm. About 3,500 aircraft were airborne, and officials said all of them landed safely.
The effects reached beyond US airports. Canadian Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon said Canada's air traffic systems were operating normally but warned that travel to the US could be disrupted. He said Canada had offered the FAA its 'full assistance', including room for US-bound aircraft.
Toronto Pearson said flights to and from the US would keep facing disruptions and cancellations even after the ground stop ended. Air Canada cancelled all its US flights for the rest of Friday evening and said the impact would continue into Saturday. Passengers were told to check with their airlines.
Bedford said he expected US air travel to return to normal by the end of Sunday, 15 November. Duffy was more cautious, saying delays and cancellations would continue as carriers 'reposition aircraft/crews where they are needed most'.
The harder questions are still open. Investigators have yet to explain how one router produced enough traffic to unsettle control centres across the country. Until investigators establish the precise cause, contractor error and faulty equipment remain possible explanations rather than confirmed findings.

sources.news_title: FAA lifts groundstop as weekend flight chaos worsens
sources.text:
Thousands more flights were canceled on Saturday after the Federal Aviation Administration lifted a nationwide groundstop that halted departures for about four hours on Friday, according to federal officials. Airlines have canceled more than 3,200 flights so far on Saturday, on top of over 9,000 on Friday. More than 800 delays were reported early Saturday, following nearly 7,000 on Friday.
Cancellations mount after Friday halt
The FAA halted departures shortly before 4 p.m. Eastern on Friday, citing extraordinary circumstances and safety concerns. Officials said more than 3,500 planes were in the air when the order took effect. Airports became gridlocked with too many aircraft on the ground and not enough parking space. Hundreds of flights turned back or diverted. Officials said flights would resume in a slow, controlled manner, prioritising larger passenger jets over smaller aircraft.
Friday was among the worst days this year for cancellations, according to aviation-data provider FlightAware, surpassed only by a January winter storm that caused over 11,600 cancellations in one day. Cirium, another aviation-data firm, said more than 30% of U.S. departing flights were canceled on Friday.
Officials blame outdated systems
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said at a White House press conference that an “incredibly old air-traffic control system” was to blame, pointing to telecom routers that “actually got overloaded with data.” He urged Congress to fund upgrades he estimated at $50 billion. Without an overhaul, Duffy said outages could recur, noting earlier disruptions in the Northeast in September and around Newark Liberty International Airport last year. “You will have more of these,” he said.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication so far of a cyberattack. He said the outage appeared tied to the FAA “putting patches into the system,” and that new equipment and technology were “overwhelming the older system.”
Telecom network under scrutiny
The outage appeared to be related to a telecommunications network overseen by L3Harris Technologies, according to government and industry officials. Some industry officials briefed on the matter said there were timing issues affecting data synchronisation throughout the network, which handles crucial radio and radar feeds for air-traffic controllers. An L3Harris spokeswoman did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Officials said that once the groundstop ended, the FAA was responsible for the turmoil in the nation’s airspace it oversees.
Airlines, airports and travellers feel the strain
Even with the departure ban lifted, airlines prepared for a difficult reset. Some carriers had already scrubbed most of their remaining Friday schedules. The pause left planes and crews out of place, which officials said would likely create cascading problems into the weekend. “It’s going to take us some time to unwind what’s happened,” Duffy said. He encouraged college football teams to contact the FAA to ensure their chartered jets can make weekend games.
United Airlines said it would work with customers to get them to destinations once the issue is resolved. American Airlines said: “It will be all hands on deck across American to get customers on their way as soon as possible.” Several airlines issued waivers to allow travellers to rebook without penalty.
At some airports, including New York’s LaGuardia, travellers waited in long lines to retrieve checked bags before heading home. At Newark, security lines were empty as people checked phones for updates. At Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, ground traffic appeared to stop on the tarmac late Friday, and by early evening telecom systems at some FAA facilities were coming back online.
Travellers reported disrupted plans. Brooklyn musician John Sturino said he would miss a percussion convention in Indianapolis and sought a refund at a Delta lounge desk in LaGuardia. “It wasn’t worth staying in the airport,” he said. Sara Garven, 66, was stranded in Baltimore during a layover on a trip home to Wisconsin from Sarasota, Florida. She said overhead announcements every 30 minutes offered no more detail than online updates. “Our main concern is just getting home safely,” she said.
Context
This is the second time in recent years the FAA has taken the extraordinary step of halting all departures across the country. In 2023, a nationwide groundstop was ordered.
